assessment.security_status_cs: Situace v oblasti Rudého moře a Perského zálivu zůstává kritická kvůli probíhajícím útokům na ropné tankery a infrastrukturu, včetně nedávného úderu na budovu Aramco v Rijádu ze strany Houthiů. Uzavřený Hormuzský průliv a přetrvávající napětí mezi USA a Íránem drží globální trhy v pohotovosti navzdory mírnému nárůstu dodávek.
assessment.security_status_en: The situation in the Red Sea and Persian Gulf remains critical due to ongoing attacks on oil tankers and infrastructure, including a recent strike by Houthis on the Aramco building in Riyadh. The closed Strait of Hormuz and persistent US-Iran tensions keep global markets on high alert despite a slight recovery in oil flows.

recommendations.reason_en: Persistent threats and attacks in key corridors force shipping companies to use longer routes, maintaining high freight rates and profitability.

recommendations.reason_en: Risks associated with the closed Strait of Hormuz and attacks on energy infrastructure in the Persian Gulf support rising oil prices and corporate margins.

articles.title: Netanyahu sought private talks with Palestinian party leader despite public attacks
articles.summary:
Netanyahu sought private talks with Palestinian party leader despite public attacks

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 11:17
Mansour Abbas says the prime minister's speech vilifying Palestinian parties put him at risk
Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu looks on during a speech on the opening day of the new Israeli parliament in Jerusalem on 10 November 2026 (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP)
Off

The leader of the United Arab List, Mansour Abbas, said on Wednesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had held private talks with him through a close associate, despite publicly branding Palestinian parties "terror supporters who hate Israel".

"He was interested in our position on the law barring an indicted lawmaker from serving as prime minister, and whether we really intended to enter a coalition and replace Netanyahu's government," Abbas told Kan public radio.

"When it serves his interests, Arab citizens suddenly become legitimate, he becomes 'Abu Yair', and Mansour Abbas becomes a worthy partner in his eyes."

The Palestinian-led United Arab List (Ra'am) and the Joint List won a record 19 seats combined, following a surge in turnout among Palestinian voters in Israel, giving them the balance of power.

In a speech to parliament on Tuesday evening, Netanyahu said the United Arab List and the Joint List were seeking to end Israel’s existence, adding that the two parties disagreed only on "what kind of state will arise on its ruins".

"What is the true goal of these factions?" Netanyahu said. "Is it only to improve the socioeconomic conditions of Arab citizens in Israel? We have no problem with that. But that is not their real goal."

Addressing those considering forming a government with Palestinian parties, Netanyahu added: "Don't you understand what they really want to achieve? What their national aspiration is?"

Abbas said Netanyahu’s speech had put him and his family in danger. Asked whether he had received threats, Abbas replied: "There are threats from several directions."

Nearly 80 percent of Britons see Israel as a threat to world peace
Read More »

"As a party, we have made peace one of our core principles," Abbas said. "To accuse us of supporting terrorism is simply false and always has been. We are law-abiding citizens."

In an interview with Channel 12, Abbas also rejected Netanyahu’s claims about his party’s objectives.

"We do not want to establish an Islamist state or an Arab state," he said. "We have defined ourselves as citizens within the State of Israel. We support peace and ending the conflict through a two-state solution."

Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader tasked by the president with forming a government, described Netanyahu’s speech as "delusional, divisive, hateful and disgraceful".

His Yashar party said it had scheduled coalition talks with Netanyahu’s Likud party, but cancelled the meeting following the prime minister’s address.

"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," Eisenkot wrote in a post on X. 

"I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."

articles.title: Egypt deployed forces to Saudi Arabia before Sisi's public pledge of military support, sources say
articles.summary:
Egypt deployed forces to Saudi Arabia before Sisi's public pledge of military support, sources say

Submitted by MEE correspondent on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 11:10
Egypt sent troops, Rafale fighter jets, helicopters and transport aircraft to the kingdom despite major disagreements within the military's top brass over Cairo's role in the conflict
Egyptian army special forces can be seen in northern Sinai province on 20 October 2023 (Kerolos Salah/AFP)
On

Egypt deployed forces and military aircraft to Saudi Arabia and moved air defence systems to strategic locations across the country long before President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi publicly pledged Cairo's support for Riyadh, Egyptian military sources have told Middle East Eye.

The deployment included a squadron of Rafale fighter jets, eight helicopters and four large transport aircraft, an Egyptian military source said on condition of anonymity as he was not authorised to speak with the media.

Egyptian naval warships had also moved towards the southern Red Sea, near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, the source added.

The reported naval movements came amid growing Egyptian concern over the security of Red Sea shipping lanes and the threat posed by Houthi attacks in Yemen.

In August, Egypt reportedly increased its naval presence near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, with reports claiming that modern frigates and corvettes had been deployed towards the southern entrance of the Red Sea.

Separately, Al Jazeera Arabic's open-source investigations unit reported last month that flight-tracking data had identified two Egyptian military C-130 Hercules transport aircraft operating in Saudi airspace.

The aircraft, identified by their registration numbers SU-BAI and SU-BEW, were tracked over western Saudi Arabia before their signals disappeared. 

One was subsequently detected over northwestern Saudi Arabia, before its signal disappeared again while it was flying towards the Red Sea coast near Al Wajh.

One of the military sources told MEE that Egypt had also repositioned several air defence systems, including Skyguard-Amoun batteries, to strategic locations in the east and south of the country.

"Security discussions and exchanges between the two countries had been ongoing since the fighting began, with the aim of agreeing on how military intervention and support would be carried out," the source said.

"While Egyptian-Saudi military cooperation had been agreed upon, the strategy, mechanisms and operational plans for intervention were still being discussed and coordinated to maintain Egypt's national security," he added.

Abdelatty confirms deployment

On Monday, hours after MEE sent Egypt's foreign ministry a request for comment, Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty confirmed that the Egyptian military had been deployed to Saudi Arabia before Sisi obtained parliamentary approval. 

"Our presence there began a few months ago after the attacks and aggressions on Saudi Arabia during the escalation with Iran," Abdelatty told France 24, adding that Cairo was now in the process of "strengthening" that deployment.

On 17 October, Sisi called for parliament to authorise the deployment of Egyptian forces to defend Saudi Arabia if requested. 

The following day, the National Defence Council, chaired by the president, announced that Egypt would provide all possible support to protect the kingdom's security and territorial integrity.

'Our presence there began a few months ago after the attacks and aggressions on Saudi Arabia during the escalation with Iran'

- Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty

Under Article 152 of Egypt's constitution, the president must consult the National Defence Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of the House of Representatives before sending the armed forces on a combat mission outside the country.

Parliament held closed sessions on 18 and 19 October before reconvening on 26 October, when lawmakers approved Sisi's request by a two-thirds majority.

The authorisation allows the president to take necessary measures, in coordination with the kingdom, to defend its territory against external aggression.

The parliamentary approval, however, has not publicly clarified the precise nature or extent of Egypt's military commitment.

The disclosures come as Saudi Arabia faces renewed missile and drone attacks by Yemen's Houthi movement, with the escalation increasingly drawing regional powers into discussions over the kingdom's defence.

On Sunday, a building linked to Saudi state oil giant Aramco in Riyadh sustained minor damage after being struck by falling debris from an intercepted attack. No casualties were reported.

The incident followed a series of Houthi attacks on Saudi territory, including strikes targeting strategic infrastructure, prompting Riyadh to seek additional military and diplomatic support from regional allies.

The Saudis have escalated strikes against Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, with dozens of casualties reported.

Divisions over ground intervention

A second senior Egyptian military official, also speaking on condition of anonymity, described sharp disagreements within the country's military leadership over the scope of any intervention, particularly whether Egyptian ground troops should participate in operations against the Houthis in northern Yemen.

The official said meetings involving Sisi, commanders from different branches of the armed forces and members of the National Defence Council had been marked by disputes over the possibility of sending ground forces into Yemen.

"The meetings witnessed arguments over the deployment of ground troops in operations planned to take place in northern Yemen against the Houthis," the official said.

According to the source, Sisi pushed for Egypt to participate in Saudi military operations, arguing that further delays were difficult to justify as attacks on the kingdom continued to escalate.

Yemen war: Why Egypt's vow to defend Saudi Arabia is a risky gamble
Read More »

"Saudi Arabia had officially requested Egyptian military support in the current war. It was in Egypt's security interests to take part in the operations to safeguard water security and protect the Red Sea and the Suez Canal," the source said.

"Saudi economic support for Egypt is also part of the objectives behind the Egyptian move," the source added.

The source also pointed to Cairo's financial relationship with Riyadh, which has become an important dimension of bilateral ties.

On 30 October, Egyptian media outlets, citing banking sources, reported that Saudi Arabia had agreed to renew a $5.3bn deposit at the Central Bank of Egypt for another year, shortly before it was due to mature.

The deposit forms part of Saudi Arabia's wider financial support for Egypt, which has faced persistent pressure on its foreign currency reserves and economy.

The renewal came less than two weeks after Sisi publicly pledged to defend Saudi Arabia, although there has been no public evidence establishing a direct connection between the financial arrangement and Cairo's military decision.

The debate over the possible deployment of Egyptian ground troops also reflects wider regional efforts to strengthen Saudi Arabia's defences.

In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, committing the three countries to treat an armed attack against any one of them as an attack against all.

Turkey's parliament subsequently ratified the agreement in November, although this does not in itself establish that Turkish combat troops will be deployed to Yemen. The precise nature of any Turkish or Pakistani military contribution to Saudi Arabia has not been publicly established.

Ground troops remain a red line

For now, Egypt's publicly declared commitment is to support Saudi Arabia's defence. Whether this could eventually extend to Egyptian ground forces entering Yemen remains unclear.

The first military source who disclosed the deployments to MEE did not rule out Egyptian troops joining the fighting in its final phase, after air and naval operations had weakened the Houthis' military capabilities.

"Egyptian ground intervention could take place as part of a multinational ground force, rather than through Egyptian troops alone, along the lines of what happened during the 1991 Gulf War," the source said.

He stressed, however, that "a ground war was not an option at present".

"The current situation first required dealing with the Houthis' command and control centres, missile and drone launch platforms, and air defence systems before any ground engagement or even consideration of a ground war," he explained.

Sisi's 2030 exit plan would keep Egypt in the army's hands
Read More »

Earlier this month, MEE reported that the Houthis had launched multiple cross-border raids targeting Saudi military positions over the previous month, marking the first such incursions into Saudi territory since the collapse of a ceasefire in Yemen.

The small-scale raids targeted border posts in Saudi Arabia's rugged mountainous southwest, according to Arab and western officials.

The first military source said a ground offensive could ultimately be avoided if air and naval operations succeeded in weakening the Houthis' military infrastructure.

"If the air and naval operations achieved major successes, a ground offensive could instead be carried out by Yemeni forces supporting the country's internationally recognised government, without foreign ground troops," he said.

He estimated that fighting could last between four and six months before its outcome became clear, although he cautioned that the conflict could continue for longer depending on the scale of the air and naval campaign, the targets struck and whether the forces involved managed to neutralise Houthi air defences.

The second military official, however, offered a markedly different account of the discussions, saying commanders of the armed forces and members of the National Defence Council had agreed that Egypt should stay out of ground operations in Yemen.

The disagreement is rooted partly in Egypt's own experience of military intervention in the country.

Under former president Gamal Abdel Nasser, Egypt intervened in Yemen's civil war in 1962, deploying tens of thousands of troops to support republican forces fighting royalist forces backed by Saudi Arabia.

The campaign became a costly and protracted military engagement for Cairo, with thousands of Egyptian soldiers killed before the withdrawal of its forces was completed in 1970.

articles.summary:
PM, in response to Ed Davey at PMQs, says measures could help address ‘poisonous politics’

Here are some more comments on the report for the Casey commission released today looking at how social care is run in England. (See 9.56am.)

This is from Natasha Curry, deputy director of research at the Nuffield Trust and one of the report’s authors.

Compared to the other countries we looked at, the governance of England’s social care system is confused and complex. Overlapping and unclear roles leave dangerous uncertainty around who is responsible for important decisions, contributing to the inertia around reform England has struggled with for decades. The serious consequences of this were laid bare during the Covid pandemic.

The system for governing adult social care in England has evolved haphazardly and with little clear planning. That has been exacerbated by successive governments ducking politically unpalatable decisions for decades. That has scattered responsibility for the sector across and outside government in a way that few would design from scratch.

This report makes for sober reading of how adult social care and those who rely on it have been systematically failed. The fragmentation we see today is what happens when there is a total absence of political leadership to ensure the sector is well-funded and provides equitable access to care.

[Burnham] struggled to dampen splits among cabinet ministers, which were first revealed by The i Paper, who used the meeting to express differing views on the future relationship with Brussels.

One source with knowledge of the cabinet discussion said there was a “clear divide between those who want to go further and those who don’t want to push the issue too far”.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth survives effort to impeach him | First Thing
articles.summary:
House Republicans block impeachment resolution that cited US military actions in Iran, Yemen and Venezuela. Plus, SS United States to be sunk to create artificial reef

  • Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here

Good morning. House Republicans have blocked an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth. The defense secretary dismissed the impeachment resolution from a Republican lawmaker as “political spectacle”, saying it was an attempt to set up a “show trial”. Top Democrats announced their support for the resolution, but Republicans moved to kill it by referring it to the judiciary committee.

Thomas Massie’s 34-page resolution, which he read aloud on the House floor, centered on the Iran war. Hegseth said the articles targeted not just him but the troops who carried out his orders. He insisted that every operation the articles cite – including strikes on Iran and Yemen, attacks on alleged drug boats and the capture of Venezuela’s now former leader Nicolás Maduro – was lawful, ordered by Donald Trump and notified to Congress.

Why has the US Treasury chief reportedly moved? Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington area to a military base after an Iranian threat against his life, the New York Times reported. Bessent has led ‌the US sanctions and economic pressure campaign against Iran, called Operation Economic Outcast, since August.

articles.title: A journey down Egypt's Red Sea coast to find Sufi saints and a mystical lyre
articles.summary:
A journey down Egypt's Red Sea coast to find Sufi saints and a mystical lyre

Submitted by Sean Mathews on Mon, 11/09/2026 - 10:44
El-Quseir once welcomed explorers, warriors and Hajj pilgrims, but today its bypassed in favor of bigger Red Sea resorts
El-Quseir is filled with crumbling Ottoman-era houses with protruding wooden balconies (MEE/Sean Mathews)
Off

El-Quseir is pitch black at night. The only light inside this decaying labyrinth of a port comes when a battered Bajaj motorcycle purrs down the odd alley, casting a headlight on one of the town’s many stray dogs, or a passerby flashes a phone, lighting up a decaying wooden balcony.

The old mayor’s house is easy to find in the darkness. It emits a warm, golden light. When I arrive, a crowd is already gathered on the colonnaded veranda; some men in djellabas, others in the uniform skinny jeans of the Middle East.

I spot the odd Cairo hipster among them. The women attendees are especially radiant in make-up. Why shouldn’t they be.

Tonight is a Hazz night, the name, which in Arabic means luck, given to soirees down Egypt’s Red Sea coast, where the simsimiyya, a triangular lyre, is played to ballads about old ports, friendships and legendary seafarers.

The simsimiyya looms large over El-Quseir.

“The men here would be at sea for four months at a time. They would save a spot on their dhow just for a simsimiyya player to entertain them,” Aly El-Sayed, the founder of Bahar, a community organisation working to preserve the city's heritage and marine ecosystem, told me.

Aly is the host of tonight’s gathering. The old mayor’s house, a butter-yellow bungalow built in 1888, has been repurposed as Bahar’s home.

“We tried not to change much. We were even careful not to paint too much,” El-Sayed said. 

'They sang all the time'

I knew that music was central to life aboard dhows, traditional wooden sailing boats, that plied goods, including slaves, between East Africa and Arabia up until the mid-20th century.

Australian explorer Alan Villiers noted in his 1940 travel classic, Sons of Sinbad, the pride his dhow’s nokhada (captain) took in having a musician aboard ship .

The crew was musically inclined, Villiers said: “They sang continually…they sang all the time they worked and when the jobs were really big - such as hoisting the lateen yard - they stopped occasionally and danced.”

But I had only recently learned about the simsimiyya, an intimidating looking instrument made of five or six strings whose shape recalls the head of a horned gazelle. 

Sayed and his team have spent months collecting and recording songs that the seamen of Sons of Sinbad would have recognised.

Posters are arranged on the veranda that display songs with titles like Ras Gharib, Oh So Many Nights and Our Coasts Sing. 

Sayed spends some time working the crowd, nearly all of whom he knows from El-Quseir. Eventually, we take our seats.

The musician enters, dignified in a white djellaba and cradling an understated simsimiyya.

This is a far cry from the touristic players of Cairo with their microphones and flashing lights.

Our musician tucks the instrument under his arm and the crowd goes silent. His hands reach to opposite sides of the simsimiyya, as if he is holding a rifle, then they begin to dance.

His fingers are nimble but taut as he plucks and strums the strings. The notes tumble liltingly one after another and he starts his rhythmic, nasally chant about El-Quseir and the sea.

My journey started a long way from El-Quseir. I was at a dinner with a group of Egyptian writers and Yemeni expats in Cairo’s Le Bistro, a semi-subterranean, French restaurant cloistered from the chaos of downtown Cairo.

Steak frites and red Beausoleil d’Egypte wine were flowing when I asked the group, “Is Egypt more of a Mediterranean or Red Sea country?”

“Of course, Mediterranean!” one Egyptian art critic replied, almost offended.

“I’d say Red Sea, don’t forget we share the simsimiyya,” a Yemeni friend said. The table unanimously nodded in agreement.

The humble simsimiyya had silenced a cultural dispute that, in reality, has no right answer, as Egypt is an amalgam of both seas. Nevertheless, I wanted to learn more about the instrument.

My Yemeni friend recommended meeting one of the world’s leading experts on Red Sea music who happens to live in Cairo, Nizar Ghanem.

Ghanem, a Yemeni physician turned ethnomusicologist, is as much a product of the Red Sea as the simsimiyya.

Born in the port city of Aden, he spent more than two decades teaching musicology at a university in Khartoum, Sudan.

The only two countries he has called home are now ravaged by Red Sea wars. I met him at a bright apartment in Dokki where our chat was interrupted by the crack of Egyptians shooting clay pigeons at the nearby sporting club.

Port dances

For more than an hour, as I sipped delicious kiwi juice, Ghanem regaled me with the intricacies of the simsimiyya, its songs, and dances, all while explaining how they are unique to Red Sea states.

“The earliest form of a lyre we know was discovered in Mesopotamia or modern-day Iraq,” Ghanem told me.

Ancient Egypt also had lyres, but the simsimiyya as it is known today likely originated in Sudan and the Nile valley basin of Upper Egypt.

By the mid 1860s, it had moved north to Suez with migrant labourers building the canal. Between 1967 and 1982 the simsimiyya was a symbol of resistance to Israel’s occupation of Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula.

“The simsimiyya belongs to the Red Sea,” Ghanem said. “The lyrics to the songs are similar across Red Sea ports."

For example, Suakin and Yanbu both have songs about merchants from Hadhramaut,” he told me, referring to the historic ports of modern-day Sudan and Saudi Arabia respectively, and the Yemeni region whose merchants are renowned for their business acumen.

“The dances that accompany the simsimiyya in coastal areas are feminine dances. You can expect to see them in Port Sudan but not Khartoum, and in Mocha but not Sanaa,” he said.

“They are port dances. Some symbolise the struggle between man and fish."

I was already planning to visit a friend’s hotel on the Red Sea coast. Without knowing about my interest in the simsimiyya, he put me in touch with Sayed from Bahar, who, as luck would have it, was arranging a simsimiyya night.

El-Quseir is passed over by visitors to Egypt’s Red Sea coast in favour of monstrous resort hubs like Sharm el-Sheikh or Marsa Alam, but that wasn’t always the case. In the 1st century AD, the port’s name was Myos Hormos.

An unknown Greek-speaking traveller records it in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a historic account of the region's ancient trading ports. 

El-Quseir’s place as a trading hub was due to its geography.

The port sits at the eastern terminus of a series of wide, flat wadis, which were thoroughfares connecting the fertile Nile Basin to the Red Sea.

The Nile juts eastward at the same latitude as El-Quseir, which makes it the shortest distance to the river along the coast. The Nile is the rich hinterland - in food and people - of Egypt’s unforgiving Red Sea coast. Still today, many hotel workers on the coast hail from Luxor.

Egypt’s economy is heavily indebted and it has been hit by external shocks, including on the Red Sea, where Yemeni Houthi attacks have hurt traffic through the Suez Canal, which contributes precious hard currency to Cairo's coffers. But real-estate development - in part as a hedge against inflation - is booming.

To get to El-Quseir from Cairo, I flew to Hurghada. The highway south out of Hurghada is peppered with billboards offering down payment plans on beachside resorts, beckoning buyers with crystal-clear water.

Driving south, the Red Sea hills to the west rise like shards of brownish-red glass. There is no natural transition between the desiccated, Eastern Desert and the shore. Mushrooming villas and hotels are surrounded by country-club green grass and imported palm trees.

The busiest stretch of road between Hurghada and El-Quseir is at Safaga, a key Red Sea port, where lorries stretch for hundreds of metres.

James Bruce's Red Sea journey 

There are few redeeming qualities to El-Quseir’s outskirts. The city is ringed by red-brick tenements framed in concrete whose rooftops are peppered with plastic water tanks. But on Port Said Street leading to the corniche, the old El-Quseir appears.

We drive by coral stone shops with painted wooden shutters and I peek down alleys covered by precarious timber balconies. The whole city appears to be melting away in the hot, humid Red Sea air.

I drive by the white-washed governor's palace and Sheikh el-Farran mosque, named after a holy man from modern-day Saudi Arabia who locals later told me is a patron of Red Sea sailors. My hostel boasts the finest architecture in the port.

The El-Queseri hotel is three stories of rough-hewn, honey coloured coral stone. For $28 per night I get a whitewashed double room with two large windows looking out at the sea and a shared bathroom.

The finest feature by far is a double-decker mashrabiya, or fully enclosed balcony with paned-glass windows and louvered shutters to catch the sea breeze.

​

​The house was built in 1907 by a prominent Ababda sheikh, Tawfiq Ali Mustafa. The Ababda are a Cushitic Red Sea people who belong to the Beja tribe - nomads who live across modern-day Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea. Today they claim Arabian descent and many have assimilated into town life.

The British explorer James Bruce came across the Ababda when he travelled to El-Quseir from the Nile city of Aswan in 1769. Bruce is best remembered in history for being ridiculed after he returned to Britain and reported, factually, that the diet of modern-day Ethiopia’s inhabitants, then as now, includes raw meat, although in his time, hunks of meat were cut directly from living cattle.

Bruce described El-Quseir as "a small mud-walled village, built upon the shore, among hillocks of floating sand”. He arrived with a caravan of one thousand camels loaded with wheat destined for Mecca and guarded by 400 Ababda warriors armed with javelins.

El-Quseir’s trade was at the mercy of Ababda Bedouin who could attack caravans from the Nile. “The whole town was in terror at the influx of so many barbarians who knew no law whatever,” Bruce wrote.

I left the hotel for a meeting with a local historian, Taha Elgohary.

We agreed to meet at El-Quseir’s Heritage Preservation Association, which is housed in an old hospital built by an Italian company that mined phosphate here between 1910 and 1945.

Elgohary's family came to the city from Upper Egypt to work in the mines. After the company was nationalised and the Italians left, the management had trouble finding local workers. “The Quseir people were merchants and the Ababda were Bedouin. They didn’t want to work in a mine,” he said.

“I was born underground, in a phosphate mine,” Elgohary tells me, proudly, when we meet. “The Italians did good things for the local economy here. The people of Quseir got along well with them. King Farouk and his father King Fuad visited Quseir.”

​

​

​

​

​

​The Red Sea is littered with ports whose fortunes ebbed and flowed with the rise and fall of one empire or commodity. Phosphate mining revived the city after it fell into a period of steep decline following the opening of the Suez Canal which rewired Egypt’s coastal trade flows.

Before the canal, El-Quseir’s prospects were intimately tied to the spread of Islam.

Because of its geography, El-Quseir was a hub for the export of grain from Egypt to Mecca and Medina, as well as a departure point for Hajj pilgrims.

When the rulers of Cairo were established and could ensure security in Upper Egypt, the city benefited, as it did under the Ayyubid dynasty and early Mamluk empires.

The Ottoman conquest of Egypt in 1517, and maritime rivalry with the Portuguese made Red Sea ports strategic assets. But when Bruce arrived, El-Quseir was in one of its periods of decline. 

Napoleon in Egypt

Egypt, although nominally part of the Ottoman Empire, had drifted back into Mamluk control. The Mamluks were a strange class of white slave-warriors taken from the Caucasus at boyhood and converted to Islam.

By the late 1700s, as the writer Alan Moorehead observed in his classic The Blue Nile, the Mamluks were a “worn-out military clique of medieval backwardness”.

Their vulnerabilities tempted Napoleon, who invaded Egypt in 1798 in a daring bid to threaten the British in India via the Red Sea. El-Quseir’s strategic importance emerged during the war when Ottoman Janissaries began landing there from Jeddah to attack Napoleon’s forces. The French conquered El-Quseir in 1799 and remained there until 1800.

​

​

​

​

​

​

​

​Elgohary told me that the best period of time in the city's modern history was when Mohammed Ali Pasha, an Ottoman merchant from the city of Kavala in modern-day Greece, consolidated power in Egypt in the early 1800s.

“The city of Quseir today is a legacy of Mohammed Ali. He built new markets and houses. He promoted business and trade with Mecca and Medina,” Elghohary told me.

Mohammed Ali tamed the Bedouin tribes and renovated an Ottoman fortress that dates back to the late 16th century. When his son, Ibrahim Pasha, went to fight Wahhabis in modern-day Saudi Arabia, he departed from El-Quseir. At the peak of its success, 30,000 pilgrims transited through the port each year on Hajj.

Religion and music molded by the Red Sea

After my meeting with Elghoray, I wandered the old town in a circuitous route back to my hostel. I stumbled upon whole walls of collapsed coral stone and plaster facades weather-beaten by the scorching, salty sea air.

Above me, many buildings still retained their timber balconies in faded shades of turquoise or emerald. Their humble lattice-work is just high enough to hide the women-folk of the household who would sit outside and catch the sea breeze.

One of the legacies of being a Hajj port is that El-Quseir attracted pilgrims from across the Islamic world.

Some died here or left offspring behind, contributing to the town’s street-level cosmopolitanism, one that is a far cry from the Red Sea’s new globalised touristic cities like Hurghada.

El-Quseir is home to 20 Sufi shrines.

I walked to Nana cafe on Port Said Street to have a coffee, and passed a group of old men in djellabas sitting outside the shrine of Abd El-Qadir El-Jilani, a Persian religious wanderer. In El-Quseir, religion, as well as music, was moulded by the Red Sea.

Even today, an element of folklore and local tradition survives in the city. In the month before Ramadan, a camel parade takes place called Al-Mahmal. The camels are outfitted in cloths from the shrine in the port and paraded through the centre.

The event commemorates the arrival of the Kiswah, the black silk fabric that covers the Kaaba in Mecca, to the port. Until the 1960s the cloth was made in Cairo and was transported via ship to Mecca. In Mamluk and Ottoman times its sea journey often started in El-Quseir.

“This celebration isn’t religious or political. It serves no purpose other than celebrating the community of El-Quseir,” El-Sayed at Bahar told me the night of the simsimiyya performance.

As the simsimiyya was strummed, I thought about the similarities between tonight and that event. “The people make Quseir unique. This is the effect of the port,” El-Sayed told me.

Inside Egypt
El-Quseir, Egypt

articles.title: UN chief tells Turkey climate summit: 'This is the path to mutually assured destruction'
articles.summary:
UN chief tells Turkey climate summit: 'This is the path to mutually assured destruction'

“The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. This is the path to mutually assured destruction,” UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres told world leaders at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey on Wednesday.

The UN chief said that the slow international response to the climate crisis had put the world on this path, and that rapid action was needed to avert it.

His comments set the tone for two days of rapid-fire speeches by world leaders at the UN conference on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, Reuters reported.

Guterres pointed to rising carbon emissions, global temperatures and worsening climate-driven disasters in his speech.

“But science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder,” he said. “Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs.”

Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are seeking agreement on a plan to increase the share of electricity in global energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels.

The summit opened on Monday and has, relative to its importance, received little attention against a backdrop of numerous wars, rampant inflation and other crises.

Rapidly rising global temperatures feed into these other crises, driving conflict and competition for resources. Oil and gas companies have profited hugely from the war on Iran, which has driven up the price of fossil fuels.

archive.security_status_cs: Bezpečnostní situace v oblasti Rudého moře a Perského zálivu zůstává napjatá kvůli pokračujícím útokům Houthiů, které nově zasáhly i finanční čtvrť v Rijádu. Přestože americká diplomacie signalizuje snahu o deeskalaci a probíhají vojenské koordinace tankerů, asymetrická hrozba na klíčových námořních trasách přetrvává.
archive.security_status_en: The security situation in the Red Sea and Persian Gulf remains tense due to ongoing Houthi attacks, which recently struck Riyadh's financial district. Although US diplomacy signals efforts toward de-escalation and military tanker coordination is underway, the asymmetric threat along critical maritime routes persists.
archive.forecast_cs: V nejbližších dnech lze očekávat kolísavý vývoj na komoditních a akciových trzích, kde budou signály o diplomatickém řešení narážet na realitu pokračujících asymetrických útoků v regionu.
archive.forecast_en: Over the coming days, volatile movements in commodity and equity markets are expected as diplomatic de-escalation signals clash with the reality of ongoing asymmetric attacks in the region.

archive.security_status_cs: Bezpečnostní situace v oblasti Blízkého východu a Rudého moře zůstává vysoce napjatá kvůli pokračujícím útokům Houthiů, které nově zasáhly i klíčovou budovu Aramco v saúdském hlavním městě. Rostoucí obavy z eskalace podtrhují incidenty v Hormuzském průlivu a přetrvávající asymetrická hrozba pro globální námořní trasy.
archive.security_status_en: The security situation in the Middle East and Red Sea remains highly tense due to ongoing Houthi attacks, which recently struck a key Aramco building in the Saudi capital. Growing fears of escalation are underscored by incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the persistent asymmetric threat to global shipping lanes.
archive.forecast_cs: V nejbližších dnech lze očekávat zvýšenou volatilitu cen ropy a komodit v reakci na přetrvávající útoky v oblasti Perského zálivu a Rudého moře, přičemž investoři budou nadále bedlivě sledovat jakékoliv náznaky vojenské či diplomatické eskalace.
archive.forecast_en: Over the coming days, increased volatility in oil and commodity prices is expected in response to ongoing attacks in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, while investors will closely monitor any signs of military or diplomatic escalation.

archive.security_status_cs: Situace v oblasti Rudého moře a Perského zálivu zůstává kritická kvůli probíhajícím útokům na ropné tankery a infrastrukturu, včetně nedávného úderu na budovu Aramco v Rijádu ze strany Houthiů. Uzavřený Hormuzský průliv a přetrvávající napětí mezi USA a Íránem drží globální trhy v pohotovosti navzdory mírnému nárůstu dodávek.
archive.security_status_en: The situation in the Red Sea and Persian Gulf remains critical due to ongoing attacks on oil tankers and infrastructure, including a recent strike by Houthis on the Aramco building in Riyadh. The closed Strait of Hormuz and persistent US-Iran tensions keep global markets on high alert despite a slight recovery in oil flows.
archive.forecast_cs: V nejbližších dnech lze očekávat přetrvávající vysokou volatilitu cen komodit a ropy, podpořenou novými útoky Houthiů a napětím v oblasti Perského zálivu. Trhy budou nadále citlivě reagovat na jakékoliv zprávy o vojenské eskalaci.
archive.forecast_en: Over the coming days, continued high volatility in commodity and oil prices is expected, driven by fresh Houthi attacks and ongoing tensions in the Persian Gulf. Markets will remain highly sensitive to any news regarding military escalation.
